items.title: Writing a précis — the step-by-step method
items.body:
The paper gives a **300-word passage** and asks for a précis in **about 100 words (one-third), 15 marks**.

**Steps:**
1. **Read twice** — first for the gist, then to underline the key points.
2. **Find the central idea** — one sentence you could tell a friend.
3. **List the essential points**; strike out examples, statistics-as-illustration and repetition.
4. **Draft in your own words**, in reported speech and the third person.
5. **Trim to ~100 words**; count them.
6. **Add a short title** naming the theme — not too narrow (one detail or a personal angle), not too broad or exaggerated. For a passage arguing that study method matters more than hours, 'Study Smart, Not Just Long' works; 'The History of Examinations' does not.
7. **Check:** does it read as one connected paragraph and keep the original meaning?

| Keep | Drop |
|---|---|
| Main idea | Long examples |
| Essential reasons | Illustrations |
| Conclusion | Repetition |
| Logical links | Rhetorical flourish |
keyPoints: Précis = about one-third of the passage (100 words for 300), worth 15 marks.
Capture the central idea plus essential points; drop examples, illustration and repetition.
Write in your own words, reported speech, third person.
Present it as a single connected paragraph and add a short title.
Count words and check that the meaning is unchanged.
items.source: APPSC 07/2026 English syllabus — Précis Writing (Item 07); SSC-standard method.

items.title: Précis — do's and don'ts that decide marks
items.body:
Marks are lost on avoidable errors, not on the difficulty of the passage.

**Do:**
- Preserve the **exact meaning** and every main point.
- Use **your own words** and **linking devices** for flow.
- Keep it to **one paragraph** within the word count.
- Convert direct speech to **reported speech**.

**Don't:**
- Don't add your **own opinion** or any **new fact**.
- Don't copy **whole sentences** from the passage.
- Don't use **abbreviations** or note form.
- Don't miss a **main point** while cutting length.

**Golden rule:** a précis is a faithful miniature of the passage — smaller, but the same picture.

**Worked example — direct to reported speech.** Speech: 'I promise you all that I will fight for your rights.' Précis: **The speaker promised to fight for the listeners' rights.** What changed: *I* → *the speaker* (third person); *promise* → *promised* (past, reported); *you / your* → *the listeners'*. The meaning is unchanged — no command, no new idea.
keyPoints: Preserve the exact meaning and every main point while cutting length.
Never add personal opinion or new facts.
Do not copy whole sentences; paraphrase in your own words.
Avoid abbreviations and note form; write full connected prose.
A précis is a faithful miniature — smaller but the same picture.

items.title: Translating Telugu to English — method and word order
items.body:
The paper asks you to translate a **~150-word passage from the regional language (Telugu) to English (Item 10, 15 marks)**.

**Method:**
1. **Read the whole Telugu passage** first for meaning — do not translate line 1 before you know line 5.
2. Translate **sense-for-sense**, not word-for-word.
3. **Reorder for English syntax:** Telugu is **Subject–Object–Verb (SOV)**; English is **Subject–Verb–Object (SVO)**. Move the sentence-final verb after the subject.
4. **Add words English needs** that Telugu drops — articles *a/an/the*, and sometimes the linking verb 'is/are'.
5. **Match tense and number** to the Telugu markers (రేపు = tomorrow → future; పిల్లలు = children → plural).
6. **Re-read** the English alone — it should sound natural and mean exactly the same.

**Habits:** ప్రతిరోజూ (every day) with a verb like వెళ్తుంది shows a regular habit → English **simple present**: ఆమె ప్రతిరోజూ ఉదయం ఆరు గంటలకు నడకకు వెళ్తుంది → *She goes for a walk at six o'clock every morning.* Keep every detail (time, frequency).

*Example:* రైతు పొలంలో విత్తనాలు నాటాడు (farmer / in-field / seeds / planted) → **The farmer planted seeds in the field.**

**Word meanings across the two languages (with an English antonym):**

| English | తెలుగు | English antonym |
|---|---|---|
| scarcity | కొరత (shortage) | abundance (సమృద్ధి) |
| victory | విజయం | defeat (ఓటమి) |
| ancient | ప్రాచీన | modern (ఆధునిక) |
| increase | పెరుగుదల | decrease (తగ్గుదల) |
| poverty | పేదరికం | prosperity (సంపద / శ్రేయస్సు) |
keyPoints: Telugu→English translation is a ~150-word passage worth 15 marks.
Read the whole passage first; translate sense-for-sense, not word-for-word.
Telugu is SOV, English is SVO — move the final verb after the subject.
Add English articles (a/an/the) and linking verbs that Telugu omits.
Match tense and number to Telugu time/number markers (రేపు=future, పిల్లలు=plural).
Habitual Telugu (ప్రతిరోజూ … వెళ్తుంది) → English simple present ('She goes … every morning').
Word pairs: scarcity = కొరత ↔ abundance; victory = విజయం ↔ defeat; ancient = ప్రాచీన ↔ modern.
items.source: APPSC 07/2026 English syllabus — Translation (Item 10); SSC-standard method.

items.title: Faithful translation — register, idioms and names
items.body:
A translation is judged on **fidelity** — same meaning, same tone, **nothing added and nothing dropped** — not on length, fancy vocabulary or a word-by-word copy.

**Register (formality):** a polite Telugu request ('దయచేసి ... గలరా?') becomes a polite English one ('Could you kindly ... ?'). A formal source stays formal; a casual source stays casual.

**Idioms and proverbs:** translate by **meaning**, not literally. 'చెవిన పెట్టలేదు' (lit. 'did not put in the ear') = *paid no heed / turned a deaf ear*. Where an English idiom fits, use it.

**Proper nouns and culture terms:** keep names and festivals (transliterate) and add a short gloss only if needed — 'Sankranti (the harvest festival)'. Never swap in an unrelated Western equivalent (do not turn Sankranti into Christmas).

**Numbers, dates, quantities:** carry them across exactly.
keyPoints: Fidelity = same meaning and same register; not ornate vocabulary.
Keep the formality level: polite source → polite target.
Translate idioms/proverbs by sense; use an English equivalent where it fits.
Retain proper nouns and festival names; add a brief gloss if needed.
Never substitute an unrelated Western equivalent; carry numbers/dates exactly.

items.title: How précis and translation are marked
items.body:
Knowing the marking helps you spend effort where it scores.

**Précis (15 marks) — typical split:**
- Central idea captured — high weight.
- All main points present, none added — high weight.
- Correct length (~one-third) and one-paragraph form.
- Own words, reported speech, suitable title.
- Grammar and flow.

**Translation (15 marks) — typical split:**
- Meaning fidelity (no addition/omission) — highest weight.
- Correct English grammar and natural word order.
- Register/tone preserved.
- Idioms, names and numbers handled correctly.

**Practical tips:** keep a rough draft, then a fair copy; count words for the précis; re-read your English translation on its own to catch Telugu word order left uncorrected.
keyPoints: Précis marks reward central idea + all main points, correct length, own words, title, grammar.
Translation marks reward meaning fidelity above all, then grammar and natural order.
Register/tone and correct handling of idioms, names and numbers carry marks.
Draft rough then fair; count précis words; re-read the English translation alone.
items.source: APPSC 07/2026 English syllabus (Items 07 & 10); SSC-standard marking practice.

items.title: Summary vs précis — rules, word-count and title
items.body:
A **summary** and a **précis** both compress a passage to its essentials, but the précis in the exam is judged on **strict rules**.

**What they share:** both give the **central idea and main points in your own words**, dropping examples and repetition. A general **summary** may be loose; a **précis** is a disciplined summary marked on precise rules.

**Précis rules (the ones that score):**
1. **Word-count** — about **one-third** of the original (≈100 words for a 300-word passage). Count the words and note the number.
2. **Title** — give a short **title** naming the theme.
3. **Own words, reported speech, third person** — no copied sentences, no new ideas or opinions.
4. **One connected paragraph** that keeps the original meaning and order of ideas.

| Feature | Summary (general) | Précis (exam) |
|---|---|---|
| Length | flexible | ~1/3, counted |
| Title | optional | required |
| Form | may use notes | one paragraph, full prose |
| Rule-bound | loosely | strictly |
keyPoints: A précis is a strict, rule-bound summary; both give the central idea in your own words.
Word-count = about one-third of the passage (≈100 words for 300); count it.
Always add a short title naming the theme.
Use own words, reported speech, third person; no copied sentences, opinions or new ideas.
Write one connected paragraph that keeps the original meaning and order.
A general summary may be looser; the exam précis is judged strictly on these rules.
items.source: APPSC 07/2026 English syllabus — Précis Writing (Item 07); SSC-standard method.

items.title: Compressing without losing meaning — the précis toolkit
items.body:
**In one line:** a précis reaches one-third length mainly by **replacing wordy phrases with single words**, **merging sentences**, and **turning speech into reported form**, not by dropping main points.

**Why it is asked:** item 07 (15 marks) penalises both over-length and lost points; these tools let you cut length safely.

**Wordy phrase → one word:**

| Wordy | Concise |
|---|---|
| in spite of the fact that | although |
| due to the fact that | because |
| at this point in time | now |
| a large number of | many |
| in order to | to |
| make a decision | decide |
| in the near future | soon |
| one who cannot be defeated | invincible |

**Other tools:**
1. **Combine** two sentences that share a subject into one with a connective.
2. **Generalise** a list: "rice, wheat, maize and millets" → "food grains".
3. **Report a speech in the past tense and third person**: "I promise" → "The speaker promised".
4. **Avoid opening with "The author says" / "In this passage"** — state the ideas directly.
5. Write the **word count in brackets at the end**, for example (98 words), and the **title last**.

**Worked example:** *"In spite of the fact that a large number of farmers took loans in order to buy seeds, they could not repay them due to the fact that the rains failed."* (36 words) → *"Although many farmers borrowed to buy seeds, failed rains left them unable to repay."* (14 words). Every idea survives; only padding goes.

**Don't confuse:** **compressing** (same ideas, fewer words) with **omitting** (losing a main point) — only the first is allowed.
keyPoints: in spite of the fact that → although; due to the fact that → because; at this point in time → now.
a large number of → many; in order to → to; make a decision → decide; one who cannot be defeated → invincible.
Generalise lists: rice, wheat, maize and millets → food grains.
Report speeches in past tense and third person ("I promise" → "The speaker promised").
Do not open with "The author says"; write the word count in brackets at the end, title last.
items.source: APPSC Notification 07/2026 — English (Qualifying) items 07 & 10; Wren & Martin précis chapter; SSC-standard translation practice

items.title: Telugu→English translation traps — postpositions, honorifics and reported speech
items.body:
**In one line:** Telugu attaches **postpositions** to the end of a noun and uses a **respect plural**; English needs separate **prepositions** and keeps a respected single person **singular**.

**Why it is asked:** item 10 is **"Regional Language to English", ~150 words, 15 marks**; for AP candidates the regional language is Telugu, and these slips are the commonest grammar deductions.

**Postposition → preposition:**

| Telugu ending | English | Example |
|---|---|---|
| -లో | in | ఇంట్లో → in the house |
| -మీద | on | బల్ల మీద → on the table |
| -కి / -కు | to | బడికి → to school |
| -నుండి | from | ఊరి నుండి → from the village |
| -తో | with | స్నేహితుడితో → with a friend |
| -వల్ల | because of / by | వర్షం వల్ల → because of the rain |

**Respect plural (గౌరవ బహువచనం):** *ముఖ్యమంత్రి గారు వచ్చారు* uses a plural verb out of respect, but it means **"The Chief Minister arrived"** — one person, so a **singular** English subject. **గారు** may become *Shri / Mr* or simply be dropped.

**Reported speech:** Telugu marks a report with **అని** after the quoted words: *తాను వస్తానని చెప్పాడు* → **"He said that he would come."** అని → *that*, and the tense shifts back.

**How to do it:**
1. Underline every noun ending (-లో, -కి, -తో …) and pick the English preposition.
2. Check whether a plural verb is really plural or only respectful.
3. Turn అని clauses into *that*-clauses with back-shifted tense.

**Don't confuse:** **-వల్ల** (cause: *because of*) with **-తో** (company or instrument: *with*).
keyPoints: Item 10: translate a ~150-word passage from the regional language (Telugu) into English, 15 marks.
Postpositions: -లో = in; -మీద = on; -కి/-కు = to; -నుండి = from; -తో = with; -వల్ల = because of.
Respect plural: ముఖ్యమంత్రి గారు వచ్చారు = The Chief Minister arrived (singular in English).
గారు → Shri/Mr or dropped.
అని marks reported speech → "that" with back-shifted tense (He said that he would come).
items.source: APPSC Notification 07/2026 — English (Qualifying) items 07 & 10; Wren & Martin précis chapter; SSC-standard translation practice
